# Rice 101

Get the rice right and you are most of the way to a great plate. This short
chapter is the one piece of technique that pays off in every recipe that follows.

## Know your grain

| Type | Character | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Long-grain (basmati, jasmine)** | Cooks up separate, fluffy, low-stick | Biryani, Kabsa, Hainanese, most pilafs |
| **Medium-grain (bomba, Valencia, Calrose)** | Creamier, holds sauce, slight cling | Arroz con Pollo, paella-style dishes |
| **Short-grain (Japanese, glutinous)** | Sticky, tender | Oyakodon's bed of rice, congee |
| **Parboiled / converted** | Extra-firm, forgiving | Jollof, Jambalaya, big-batch cooking |

There is no "best" rice — only the right rice for the dish. Reach for the type a
recipe calls for and it will behave the way the tradition expects.

## The two habits that fix most rice

### 1. Rinse (almost) always

Rinsing long-grain rice under cool water until it runs *nearly* clear washes off
surface starch that otherwise glues the grains together. Swirl, drain, repeat
three or four times. The exceptions are dishes where you *want* creaminess —
risotto, paella, and congee — where you skip the rinse on purpose.

### 2. Soak basmati

For biryani and Persian rice, soak rinsed basmati for 30 minutes before cooking.
The grains hydrate evenly and elongate dramatically instead of snapping. Drain
well before it hits the pot.

## Foolproof absorption rice

This is the baseline method behind most pilaf-family dishes.

::: {.callout-note}
## Ratios, by grain
- **Basmati (soaked):** 1 cup rice : 1.25 cups liquid
- **Jasmine:** 1 cup rice : 1.25 cups liquid
- **Medium-grain:** 1 cup rice : 1.5 cups liquid
- **Parboiled:** 1 cup rice : 2 cups liquid

Volumes assume a cup of ~180 g rice. When in doubt, weigh.
:::

1. Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear; drain well.
2. Combine rice, measured liquid, and salt in a heavy pot with a tight lid.
3. Bring to a boil, uncovered, then immediately drop to the lowest heat and
   cover. **Do not lift the lid.**
4. Cook 12–15 minutes (long-grain) until the liquid is gone and steam holes
   appear on the surface.
5. Off the heat, keep it covered and **rest 10 minutes**. This step is not
   optional — it lets the grains finish on residual steam and firm up.
6. Fluff gently with a fork, lifting rather than stirring, to keep grains intact.

## The two failures, diagnosed

- **Gluey / mushy:** too much water, or you stirred it. Next time cut the liquid
  by 10% and leave it alone.
- **Crunchy / dry:** too little water or heat too high (the water boiled off
  before the grain hydrated). Add a splash of hot water, re-cover, and give it
  five more minutes off direct high heat.

## Bonus: the crust is a feature

In many of these cuisines the prized part is the crisp golden crust that forms
at the bottom of the pot — Persian **tahdig**, Spanish **socarrat**, Senegalese
**xoon**. It comes from a few extra minutes on slightly higher heat at the very
end, often with a little more fat. We'll build it deliberately in the
[Zereshk Polo](zereshk-polo.qmd) chapter.
